overview.text: The spine, also called the vertebral or spinal column, is the flexible bony framework running from the neck to the tailbone. It supports the head and trunk, helps the body bend and move, and provides attachment points for muscles and ribs. Openings through the vertebrae line up to form the spinal canal, which protects and provides a passage for the spinal cord; the cord is not the same structure as the spine. In adults, the column has 24 separate vertebrae above the sacrum and coccyx, which form from fused vertebrae. Its natural curves and cushioning discs help combine support with movement.

key_facts.text: The 24 separate adult vertebrae are grouped as 7 cervical (neck), 12 thoracic (rib-bearing), and 5 lumbar (lower-back) vertebrae.
The sacrum forms from five fused sacral vertebrae, and the coccyx (tailbone) typically forms from four fused coccygeal vertebrae.
A typical vertebra has a weight-bearing body and an arch; the aligned openings in the arches make the spinal canal.
Discs between neighboring vertebral bodies provide padding and allow movement; MedlinePlus also describes them as shock absorbers during activities such as walking and jumping.
The spine has four natural curves that contribute to its strength and flexibility; scoliosis refers to an abnormal sideways curve with twisting.
